The verb to skewer has two meanings — one literal, one figurative. Both are important, widely used, and deeply connected to each other.
Meaning 1: To Pierce Something with a Sharp, Pointed Stick

When you skewer something literally, you push a long, sharp, thin stick straight through it — usually food — to hold it together or prepare it for cooking.

Picture a kebab. You take a long metal or wooden stick (called a skewer) and push it through chunks of meat, onions, and peppers so they all stay together on one stick, which can then be grilled over a flame. That act of stabbing and threading the food onto the stick is called skewering.

The key ideas are: piercing, impaling, and threading — the sharp object goes all the way through the thing. It is not a gentle action. It is direct, deliberate, and complete.

Examples:

  • "She skewered the chicken pieces and placed them on the grill."
  • "He skewered the shrimp and brushed them with garlic butter."

You can also use it more broadly for any act of stabbing or piercing with a sharp object:

  • "The arrow skewered the wooden target."
Meaning 2: To Criticize Someone Sharply, Precisely, and Devastatingly

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in everyday English — in journalism, satire, book reviews, political commentary, and casual conversation. It is also one of the most vivid and powerful verbs in the English language for describing criticism.

When you skewer someone figuratively, you criticize, mock, or expose them in a way that is sharp, precise, and completely effective. The person or thing being skewered is left looking foolish, dishonest, or weak — with no real defense remaining.

Think of it this way: just like a physical skewer pierces straight through a piece of meat, a figurative skewering pierces straight through someone's false image, flawed argument, or hypocrisy — fully exposing what is underneath.

Where you'll see this meaning most:

In satire and comedy — A comedian skewers a politician by mocking their hypocrisy so accurately and wittily that the audience laughs and the politician looks utterly ridiculous.

In reviews and criticism — A film critic skewers a bad movie by identifying every flaw with precision and wit, leaving the film's reputation in ruins.

In journalism and debate — A journalist skewers a company's false claims by presenting undeniable facts that destroy those claims one by one.

Examples:

  • "The comedian skewered the senator's speech, exposing three obvious contradictions in it."
  • "Her review skewered the novel so thoroughly that sales collapsed."
  • "The documentary skewered the corporation's environmental record."
The Emotional Weight and Tone of the Word

"Skewer" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of ruthlessness and complete effectiveness.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The journalist criticized the mayor." → sounds mild, ordinary
  • "The journalist skewered the mayor." → sounds devastating, total, and final

The word skewered tells you that the criticism not only landed — it went all the way through. This also means you would not say someone "skewered" a target if the criticism was weak, vague, or ignored. Skewering always implies the attack worked.

The word also carries a slightly dramatic, forceful quality. It is a strong choice. When a writer chooses "skewer" instead of "criticize" or "mock," they are signaling that what happened was sharp, precise, and left no escape.
The Connecting Thread Between Both Meanings

Both meanings share exactly the same core idea: something sharp going straight through something, leaving it fully exposed and vulnerable.

A metal stick goes through a piece of meat → it is pierced, held up, and completely exposed.
A sharp argument goes through someone's credibility → they are pierced, held up, and completely exposed.

The image is the same. The only difference is whether you are talking about food on a grill or a person's reputation in public discourse. Once you hold that image in your mind — a sharp point going cleanly and completely through something — you will never forget what to skewer means.
